To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) water and ions are preferentially transported along preferred pathways in a root, (ii) the preferred pathways are determined by the relative permeabilities of the root tissues and developmental zones, (iii) the preferred pathways for ion transport are different to those of water, and (iv) the preferred pathways change with time as the root grows.

(1) the Casparian band and the endodermis are the most effective barriers to water and ion flow in the root; (2) the peak in passive ion and water uptake occurs at the start (base) of the differentiation zone and (3) the level of transpirational flow has a significant impact in the differentiation zone on the uptake of water and ions, but has little effect in the elongation and transition zone.
the root is not a simple cylinder but rather a complex structure with different tissues and zones.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the passive transport of ions and water in the different zones of root development.
the modeling of passive transport in plant roots, with particular attention to the role played by the root differentiation zones.
the development of models of passive transport of water and ions in the root zone, and the use of these models to provide insight into the active uptake mechanisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the root is an active and complex organ that is able to adapt to its environment.
the root has the ability to regulate its own water and nutrient uptake.
, under the assumptions of our model, the Casparian strips and suberin lamella are not the primary barriers for the uptake of water and ions in the elongation and differentiation zones of a root.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the root has evolved to be a highly efficient device for the uptake and transport of water and ions.
the root is a highly complex structure that exhibits a high degree of radial and longitudinal differentiation.

the root zone effects on preferred pathways for the passive transport of ions and water are complex and can be understood by the combination of a model of ion transport through a root with an understanding of root anatomy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the transport properties of the root are strongly dependent on the developmental stage of the root and that this dependence should be taken into account when modeling root uptake.
the root is not a simple passive conduit for water and ions, but rather is a complex organ with a variety of transport pathways that can influence the transport of ions and water.
the root is an active and highly dynamic system and that a simple model of ion and transport in a root will not be able to capture the complex dynamics of the transport of ions and water in roots.
